The market's strength is broadening beneath the surface:

The S&P 500 Equal-Weight Index has outperformed the S&P 500 by +4.0 percentage points so far in October, on track for its 2nd-strongest monthly relative outperformance since April 2009.

This follows underperformance of -4.7 percentage points in the prior month, the weakest relative monthly return since March 2020.

By comparison, the Equal-Weight Index outperformed the S&P 500 by +4.2 percentage points in April.

So far this month, the Equal-Weight Index has gained +4.3%, while the S&P 500 has increased +0.3%.

Year-to-date, the Equal-Weight Index is up +13.4%, while the S&P 500 is up +12.1%, suggesting broader market participation.

Market leadership is broadening.

BREAKING: Brazil's -19.8% stock market crash on Monday was one of the rarest market events in the last two decades, according to our analysis.

Brazil's EWZ ETF plunged -19.8% on October 26th, marking an 8.4 standard deviation move.

For context, the ETF's average daily move over the last 20 years has been just +0.04%, with a standard deviation of 2.36%.

Under a normal distribution, the probability of a decline this extreme is approximately 1 in 58 quadrillion.

In other words, this event should be virtually impossible under conventional statistical models.

What just happened in Brazil was *almost* impossible.

BREAKING: US households now own ~42% of the US equity market, their highest proportion since the late 1990s.

This proportion has risen +7 percentage points since 2020.

Foreign investors are the 2nd-largest owners, accounting for 18%, up from 16% in 2020.

Mutual funds rank 3rd, at 15%, down from 23% in 2020.

Meanwhile, ETF ownership has increased +3 percentage points over the last 6 years, to 10%, its highest on record.

By comparison, pension and retirement funds own 8% of the market, while hedge funds own just 1%.

Household demand for stocks is stronger than ever.

US stocks tend to rally following Midterm elections:

The S&P 500 has returned +17.2% on average in the year following Midterm elections since 1950, the strongest return of any year in the Presidential cycle.

The index has finished higher in 17 of the 19 post-Midterm years during this period.

This is also nearly quadruple the +4.6% average return recorded during midterm years, when the index finished higher in 11 of 19 years.

By comparison, the S&P 500 has returned +8.1% on average in Year 4 of the Presidential cycle, or during Presidential election years, ending higher in 16 of 19 years.

In Q4 of Midterm years, the S&P 500 has delivered an average return of +6.6% since 1950, the strongest quarterly return of the Presidential cycle.

History suggests US equities will extend their rally after Midterm elections.

For the DCF model, the battle between the numerator (cashflows) and denominator (cost of capital) has morphed into a battle between rate scares (higher rates force valuations lower) and growth scares (fears about the AI train slowing down and causing the earnings “bubble” to burst). The former produces a positive correlation between equity and bond returns, and the latter produces a negative correlation. Price discovery is always happening, and usually the climb up the stairs takes longer than the climb down.

While earnings and margins continue to boom, the cap-weighted index has struggled to get out of its own way since early June as the AI space continues to correct. The market is now broadening nicely, with 59% of stocks above both their 50-day and 200-day moving average, but you wouldn’t know it from looking at a price chart of the SPX.

For now, worries about the AI wave slowing down and becoming systemic to the economy have brought the 10-year yield back down to 5.0% and has reduced the prospect of a Fed rate hike this week. Rate worries have been replaced by credit worries (at least in high yield), so the cost of capital hasn’t really changed that much. A big question for asset allocators continues to be the value proposition of Treasuries. They are attractively priced yes, but will they provide negative correlation when we need it the most?

Retail investor options trading activity is skyrocketing.

Retail options trading activity surged to 61% of total volume on Citadel's platform last week, near its highest on record.

This proportion has risen +16 percentage points over the last 12 months.

This is also 10 percentage points above the highest level recorded during the 2020 pandemic.

Meanwhile, index and ETF options accounted for the majority of retail options activity on Thursday, with 1.7 contracts traded for every single-stock contract.

The S&P 500 ETF, $SPY, and the Nasdaq 100 ETF, $QQQ, together accounted for 47% of all retail options trades.

Retail investors are trading more options than ever.

China's 2008 is happening now.

Property investment in China dropped -21% YoY in the first 9 months of 2026, its largest decline for this period of the year on record.

This marks a deterioration from a -20% YoY decline in the first 8 months of 2026.

The latest drop is also significantly worse than the -16% decline recorded during the 2020 pandemic.

Property investment in China has now contracted every month since 2022, its longest declining streak on record.

For perspective, during the 2008 Financial Crisis, this figure never fell below +1% YoY growth.

China's property sector is experiencing a historic downturn.

Investor appetite for leverage is through the roof:

10 largest US leveraged equity ETFs have attracted +$12 billion in inflows over the last month.

This is despite the market cap of these funds falling -$20 billion over the same period.

Recent inflow growth has been led by the 3x leveraged long Semiconductor ETF, $SOXL, which attracted +$9 billion over the last 2 weeks, its largest 2-week inflow on record.

The 3x leveraged long Nasdaq 100 ETF, $TQQQ, posted +$1.3 billion in inflows, its 2nd-largest 2-week intake of 2026.

Over the last 5 months, the 10 largest US leveraged equity ETFs have attracted +$19 billion in inflows.

Investors are piling into leveraged ETFs at a record pace.

BREAKING: Global equity funds attracted +$28.2 billion in inflows in the week ending October 21st, marking their 5th consecutive weekly intake.

Over this period, these funds posted +$138.6 billion in inflows.

Asian equity funds led last week’s demand, attracting +$11.5 billion, their largest weekly intake since at least December 2022

At the same time, European and US equity funds recorded +$9.1 billion and +$5.1 billion in inflows, respectively.

Meanwhile, global technology equity funds attracted +$5.1 billion, reversing -$4.8 billion in outflows in the prior week.

Investors are buying the dip in technology stocks.
